extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy (metaphysics and ethics); scholars of Schopenhauer
extracted.subtask_description: Close philosophical exposition from Schopenhauer developing Stoic ethical principles and then the metaphysical doctrine that the body is the objectivity of the will; argues for the primacy of will over mere idea and explores consequences for individuality, causality, and ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish what depends upon us and what does not (Stoic kernel)
rubrics_metrics.description: “we should consider well and distinguish what depends upon us and what does not, and therefore entirely avoid counting upon the latter,” — presented as the kernel of Stoic philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is the Stoic starting-point for avoiding pain, sorrow, and anxiety: concentrate on what is within your control. The passage notes Stoics discussed whether to apply bonum/malum to externals or inner states (an arbitrary choice) and that such disputes produced paradoxical judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will as the sole thing dependent upon us
rubrics_metrics.description: “But that which alone is dependent upon us is the will.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer links inner contentment to the will: since external circumstances determine fortune, inner contentment (or its absence) proceeds from the will. This motivates transition to a doctrine of virtue focused on internal maxims rather than external outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeno’s ethical principle: live in harmony with oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: Zeno’s starting-point: for highest good (blessedness and spiritual peace) one must live in harmony with oneself (Consonanter vivere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires determining oneself rationally according to concepts rather than changing impressions and moods; to be consistent one must set maxims of conduct (not consequences) as the aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition: live in harmony with nature (Kleanthes/Chrysippus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Successors added the material content “to live in harmony with nature” (ὁμολογουμενως τῃ φυσει ζῃν); Kleanthes meant whole nature, Chrysippus human nature in particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expansion makes virtue that which accords with human nature (as distinct from satisfying animal desires), and so ethics is forcibly united to a doctrine of physics; Stoics aim at unity of principle between God and the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of Stoic aim of blessedness (paradox of suicide)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Stoic aim of a ‘blessed life’ is undermined by the doctrine’s recommendation of suicide in cases of incurable suffering: “its one aim, blessedness, is rendered vain, and nothing remains as a mode of escape from suffering except death.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer presents this as an inner contradiction: a system aiming to free one from suffering must still permit suicide, which casts doubt on its claim to deliver a blessed life and contrasts Stoic ideals with other doctrines (e.g., Christianity, Indian philosophy) that reject suicide and present richer forms of moral and poetic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical method limitation: cannot reach real nature from idea alone
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot arrive at the real nature of things from without; investigations that confine themselves to ideas (forms/laws) only produce images and names, not the ‘in itself.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematics (quantity) and etiology/morphology (forms and causal laws) explain structure and ordering but not the inner nature of forces; therefore another route is needed — the route via the subject’s embodied will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectification of the will: the body is the objectivity of will
rubrics_metrics.description: “The action of the body is nothing but the act of the will objectified, i.e., passed into perception.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every true, immediate act of will is simultaneously a movement of the body; act of will and bodily movement are not cause and effect but one and the same, known in two different ways (immediate willing vs perception). The body is thus the will’s objectivity and the will provides key to the body’s inner nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double knowledge / individuality: body known as idea and as will
rubrics_metrics.description: The body is given in two entirely different ways to the subject: as an idea (object among objects) and as will (immediate self-knowledge), and this double knowledge makes the knowing subject an individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction grounds the claim that our privileged access to our own body (as will) provides a key for understanding other objects; it also explains how individuality results from the special double relation to one particular idea (the body).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain and pleasure as immediate affections of will (not mere ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is quite wrong, however, to call pain and pleasure ideas, for they are ... immediate affections of the will in its manifestation, the body.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only very weak impressions of sight, hearing, touch (in a specific mode) do not affect the will and can be treated as mere ideas. Stronger impressions influence the will and thereby are not purely perceptual data; they manifest as pain (opposed to will) or pleasure (in accordance with will).

rubrics_metrics.name: Etiology and causality limited to appearance; forces remain unexplained
rubrics_metrics.description: Etiology (causal explanation) stipulates laws of appearance in space and time but “affords us absolutely no information about the inner nature of any one of these phenomena: this is called a force of nature.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causal laws enumerate regularities but do not disclose the inner nature of the forces; hence even complete etiological knowledge leaves a secret about what things are in themselves — motivating the turn to will as the inner nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Groundlessness of the will relative to sufficient reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Motives determine only what I will at this time and place; the will itself lies outside the province of the law of motivation and is to be called ‘groundless.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While motives explain particular manifestations of volition (appearance), they cannot account for the will’s inner nature or why one has a particular empirical character in general. This invokes Kant’s empirical/intelligible character distinction and frames the will as not fully explainable by the principle of sufficient reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical inference: attribute will to the external world
rubrics_metrics.description: By analogy with our double knowledge of our body, we shall assume that objects not given as our own bodies nevertheless have, in their inner nature, the same as that in us which we call will: “what remains of objects when we set aside their existence as idea ... must in its inner nature be the same ... which we call will.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer proposes using our privileged self-knowledge to analogically ascribe will as the inner reality of the material world; this is the methodological move toward construing the world as will rather than as mere idea.
